# The Great Dictators 

What do the tyrants of the 20th century have in common? Terror, confusion and quasi-religious followings.

 Frank Dikötter | Published in History Today Volume 69 Issue 10 October 2019 

Throughout the 20th century, hundreds of millions of people cheered their dictators, even as they were herded down the road to serfdom. Across the planet, the faces of Hitler, Mussolini, Mao, Stalin and others appeared on hoardings and buildings, with portraits in every school, office and factory. Ordinary people had to bow to his likeness, pass by his statue, recite his work, praise his name, extol his genius.

The glorification of a dictator has been called the cult of personality. At its heart lies a paradox: the modern dictator must create the illusion of popular support. In an age of democracy, the people are supposed to be sovereign and select their leader through an election. But dictators opt to seize power by organising a coup or by rigging the system. Power seized through violence must be maintained by violence. A dictator must rely on military forces, a secret police, a praetorian guard, spies, informants, interrogators and torturers. It is best to pretend that coercion is actually consent.

### The cult of personality

If dictators were afraid of their own people, they were even more fearful of their entourage. Alone, they were weak. Had they been strong, they would have been elected by majority. Instead, they decided to take a shortcut, often over the bodies of their opponents. But, if they could seize power, others could, too. All of them had to contend with rivals, often just as ruthless as they, waiting to take their place.

There were many strategies for getting rid of rivals, real or imagined. Bloody purges, for example, manipulation, or divide and rule. But the cult of personality was the most efficient and that with the best chances of longevity. Such ‘cults’ debased allies and rivals alike, forcing them to collaborate through common subordination. Most of all, by compelling them to acclaim him before the others, a dictator turned everyone into a liar. When everyone lies, no one can be trusted, making it difficult to find accomplices and organise a coup.

Who built up the cult? There were hagiographers, photographers, playwrights, composers, poets, editors and choreographers, powerful ministers of propaganda and sometimes even entire branches of industry. But the ultimate responsibility lay with the dictators themselves. ‘Politics in a dictatorship begins in the personality of the dictator’, wrote Mao Zedong’s doctor in a memoir.

Some intervened more often than others. Benito Mussolini, by one account, spent half of his time projecting himself as the omniscient, omnipotent and indispensable ruler of Italy – on top of running half a dozen ministries. He was a master at projecting his own image, carefully studying certain gestures and poses. He rehearsed in Villa Torlonia, a vast neoclassical villa on a sprawling estate, which became his residence in 1925. In the evenings he would sit in a comfortable chair in a projection room to study every detail of his public performance.

His theatrical gestures – head leaning halfway back, chin jutting sharply forward, rolling eyes – were calculated to give an impression of power and vitality. He showed himself to millions with whirlwind tours around the country, endless unannounced visits to villages, mass meetings with workers and inaugurations of public projects. His image was everywhere, on books, walls and fences. His speeches were widely reproduced. As Italo Balbo, one of the blackshirt leaders, put it: ‘Italy is a newspaper in which Mussolini writes the first page every day.’

Adolf Hitler, too, was a master of propaganda, at once actor, choreographer, orator and self-publicist, a man who worked tirelessly at building up his party and his image. Like Mussolini, he was short-sighted, but never appeared in public wearing his spectacles. He hired Heinrich Hoffmann as his personal photographer to produce images that projected sheer determination and fanatical willpower, showing a grim look, raised eyebrows, lips pressed together, arms resolutely folded. After 1933 Hitler worked on his broadcasting skills, making sure no one could escape his voice as loudspeaker pillars were erected in cities, mobile loudspeakers taken to small towns. Joseph Goebbels assisted him, but after he failed to exploit all the resources offered by cinema, Hitler turned to Leni Riefenstahl instead. She made him the star of a series of films shown in every theatre.

Joseph Stalin constantly pruned his own cult. He was a compulsive editor, poring over editorials, editing speeches and reviewing articles, cutting back what he thought was excessive praise only to allow it to reappear a few years later when he judged that the time was ripe. In June 1934, he began overseeing every aspect of the state propaganda machine.

Art had to glorify the revolution. Since Stalin was the embodiment of the revolution, his posters, portraits, busts and statues appeared everywhere. Five cities were named after him, as well as parks, factories, railways and canals. The constitution, passed at the height of the show trials in December 1936, was called Stalin’s Constitution. In his final days, sensing that the end was imminent, he began self-deification. In July 1951 – between purges – he commissioned a statue of himself from 33 tonnes of bronze.

In China, Mao slogans, photos, posters and books became all the rage during the Cultural Revolution. Entire branches of industry were converted to produce cult objects. Factories producing red ink for the Little Red Book worked around the clock but still ran dry. A thriving black market appeared in badges, as the national output of more than 50 million a month was insufficient. The amount of aluminium used to make the badges was so enormous that Mao issued a ban in 1969: ‘Give me back my aeroplanes.’

At the height of the Cultural Revolution, people were fighting each other in the streets with machine guns and anti-aircraft artillery, all equally certain that they represented the true voice of Mao Zedong. It seemed like chaos, but the Chairman prevailed, feeding a seemingly endless cycle of violence in which people scrambled to prove their loyalty to him and him alone. At the end of his life, towering above his colleagues with millions of lives ruined, Mao felt secure enough to order the cult to be scaled back.

### Crocodile tears

On occasion, expressions of devotion towards dictators have appeared so spontaneous that outside observers – as well as later historians – assumed they were genuine. Millions grieved when Mao died in 1976. Traditionally in China, weeping for dead relatives and even throwing oneself on the ground in front of the coffin was a required demonstration of filial piety. Sometimes actors were hired to wail loudly at the funerals of important dignitaries, thus encouraging other mourners to join in without feeling embarrassed.

Much as people had mastered the art of effortlessly producing proletarian anger at denunciation meetings, many knew how to cry on demand. But people showed less contrition in private. One young woman remembers how her father invited his closest friend to their home, locked the door and opened their best bottle of wine. The following day they went to a public memorial service where everyone cried as if they were heartbroken. ‘As a little girl, I was confused by the adults’ expressions – everybody looked so sad in public, while my father was so happy the night before.’ In North Korea the nation cried when Kim Il-sung passed away in 1994, although no one could tell who was sincere and who was not. People tried to outdo one another in displays of grief, pounding their heads, collapsing in theatrical swoons, ripping off their clothes, waving their fists at the sky in feigned rage.

Millions of people, we have been told, believed in the cults of Hitler, Stalin and Mao. But, as freedom of speech is always the first casualty of a dictatorship, it is impossible to know what citizens really thought. Within a year of coming to power, the Nazis threw some 100,000 ordinary citizens into concentration camps. The Gestapo, the Brownshirts and the courts alike did not hesitate to lock up those who failed to acclaim their leader properly.

Those dictators who lasted had many skills. Most excelled at hiding their feelings. Mussolini saw himself as Italy’s finest actor. In an unguarded moment Hitler, too, called himself Europe’s greatest performer. But in a dictatorship many ordinary people also learned how to act. They had to smile on command, parrot the party line, shout the slogans and salute their leader. In short, they were required to create the illusion of consent, condemned to enthusiasm. Those who failed to play along were fined, imprisoned and occasionally shot.

The purpose of the cult was not to convince or persuade, but to sow confusion, destroy common sense, enforce obedience, isolate individuals and crush their dignity. People had to self-censor and in turn they monitored others, denouncing those who failed to appear sufficiently sincere in their professions of loyalty. No one knew who believed what. 

### True believers

Since a cult had to appear as though it genuinely welled from the hearts of the people, it was invariably tinged with superstition and magic. In some countries the religious overtones were so striking that one might be tempted to see it as a peculiar form of secular worship. But in every case this impression was deliberately cultivated from above. Hitler presented himself as a messiah united with the masses in a mystical, quasi-religious bond. Mussolini encouraged feelings of devotion and worship characteristic of Christian piety. There were holy sites, holy pictures, pilgrimages, the hope of a healing touch from the leader. In the Soviet Union, even as the Orthodox church came under siege, a new religion under the red star appeared, with a corner dedicated to Lenin in factories, offices and restaurants, some of them real altars decorated with ribbons and wreaths.

In Haiti, François Duvalier went to great lengths to assume the air of a Voodoo priest, encouraging rumours about his otherworldly powers. He wore thick, dark spectacles and occasionally appeared in public with a top hat and tailcoat, imitating Baron Samedi, the spirit of the dead and guardian of cemeteries. He would mumble mysteriously in a deep nasal tone, as if chanting incantations against his enemies. In Ethiopia, soon after the 1974 revolution, Mengistu Haile Mariam occupied the Grand Palace, which was run as if the emperor Haile Selassie were still in residence, with chained cheetahs, lion statues and liveried footmen. After Mengistu had the emperor throttled to death and buried underneath his office, he placed his desk right above the corpse. His portrait went up everywhere, sometimes in the old imperial frames with a crown on top.

In communist regimes there was an added need for some sort of traditional resonance. The reason was simple: few people in predominantly rural countries such as Russia, China, Korea or Ethiopia understood Marxism-Leninism. Appeals to the leader as some sort of holy figure were more successful than an abstract political philosophy that a largely illiterate population in the countryside found hard to comprehend. Stalin and his acolytes understood this all too well when they decided to have Lenin embalmed and displayed on Red Square, where he was worshipped like a saint.

Loyalty to one person mattered most in a dictatorship, more so than loyalty to one creed. Ideology, after all, can be divisive. A body of work can be interpreted in different ways, potentially leading to different factions. The greatest enemies of the Bolsheviks were the Mensheviks and both swore by Marx. Mussolini spurned ideology and kept fascism deliberate
